newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-ONLY FIVE JOURNALISTS ATTEND SELES PRESS CONFERENCE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-ONLY FIVE JOURNALISTS ATTEND SELES PRESS CONFERENCE.

text.p: Since her return to competition Monica Seles has never felt completely comfortable in the tennis spotlight.
At the French Open, however, the reality is rather different. If Seles really does want to be alone, she has come to the right place.
On the first day of the tournament on Monday, the three-times champion steamrollered Japan's Miho Saeki 6-0 6-3 in just 44 minutes and hardly anyone took any notice.
When Seles was forced out of the sport for 27 months after being stabbed in the back during a tournament in Hamburg, people couldn't stop talking about her.
But now, a little over a year since her brilliant comeback, she's become almost a forgotten woman at the tournament she used to dominate.
On a pristine Parisian afternoon, Seles began her quest for a fourth title on an outside court before more empty seats than full ones.
In her post-match press conference only five out of the hundreds of journalists covering the two-week tournament were interested enough to attend.
"It doesn't matter to me," said Seles, when asked about the small crowd. "If I go out on the court I always look at the ball.
"Obviously the way Martina (Hingis) has played this year she deserves all the attention -- she hasn't lost a match yet this season."
A year on, the 23-year-old American is no longer looking over her shoulder, her problems now more physical than mental.

Like the two women ahead of her in the world rankings, defending French champion Steffi Graf and world number one, teenage Swiss phenomenon Hingis, Seles has spent most of the season struggling with injury.
Seles arrived in Paris with a strained Achilles tendon she hurt on Saturday losing to Jana Novotna in the final of the Madrid Open.
"I had it taped today and it's painful," said Seles. "but I've had this twice before so I know what I have to do."

Since her startling return with the a victory at the Canadian Open almost two years ago, Seles has been hampered by a succession of injuries including a broken finger that forced her out of Australian Open.
Saeki, playing in her first French Open, appeared overwhelmed by the experience as Seles won the first set 6-0 in just 18 minutes.
The tiny Japanese settled down in the second, even breaking Seles to go ahead 3-1.
Until then Seles had been strangely quiet and subdued.
But after giving herself a little talking to, Seles' determination along with her familiar grunting returned as she went on to claim the next five games and the match.
"It was a little bit hard to come back after playing in Madrid on Saturday," said Seles, a quarter-finalist last year. "I'm just glad I got my first match over."
"I lost some concentration and made some easy errors."
It was those momentary lapses that offered up glimpses of the lack of concentration and questionable motivation which have left her winless this season.
But while Seles may have been forgotten she cannot be overlooked.
She has played in four tournaments this year and finished runner-up three times, twice to Hingis.
"I have to be much more consistent, not make too many unforced errors which I'm having a hard time doing," said Seles. "I'm having a hard time giving away a lot of free points."
